absent: Full struct definitions and field offsets for mirror, device, chunk, bounce, and command structures.
Allocation policy for new chunks and eviction details beyond removal marking.
Bounce buffer setup, read path, write path, and unlocked read behavior.
Device selection logic and page to device mapping rules.
Device memory fault, free, folio split, and operations table behavior.
File operations for mmap, module init, exit, and device lifecycle.
Numeric values of ioctl commands, permission bits, tags, and timeout constants.
Concurrency rules for allocation counter visibility and memory ordering.

findings.text: User control arrives through an unlocked ioctl handler that validates alignment and overflow of the supplied address range, clears completion counters, and dispatches to read, write, migrate in either direction, exclusive acquisition, exclusive check, snapshot, chunk release, flag update, and unlocked read operations.

Migration toward the device proceeds in chunks bounded by virtual area limits, with setup followed by allocation and copy, page installation, device mapping, and finalization, then a verification readback under the mirror lock with results returned to the caller.

Migration toward the system proceeds in bounded chunks with setup, device to system allocation and copy, page installation, and finalization, accumulating a count of entries that remained valid and requested migration.
Address ranges derived from a base plus a page count are rejected when addition wraps, and callers obtain a reference on the mirrored address space before use and release it afterwards.

A device spin lock serializes updates to the free page list, the free folio list, and the allocation counter, with the lock held only around list manipulation and released before chunk allocation that may sleep.
A per mirror mutex serializes insertions into the device page table index and verification reads, with atomic tagged insertions and bulk migration mappings performed while holding it.
A device memory lock serializes changes to the chunk table during removal, with per chunk eviction and teardown performed while the table is stable.
The mirrored address space is examined under a read lock while migration setup, exclusive acquisition, and range faulting occur, with the lock released before user copy or extended retry loops.
Snapshot invalidation acquires the mirror mutex in blocking mode when allowed and otherwise attempts a nonblocking acquisition, reporting failure without state change when the lock is contended.
Large allocations use a huge page order and folio granularity while small allocations use single pages, with aligned runs reclaimed as folios and unaligned remainders reclaimed as pages.

Private zone device pages are paired with system backing pages through device private storage, while coherent zone pages carry no separate backing allocation and the mirror link is recorded in the backing page.
A one shot failure flag forces the next allocation attempt to fail and then clears itself, exercising fallback to smaller pages or error propagation without retry of the failed unit.

Device to system fault handling preserves write and compound attributes, prefers a large system allocation when the source order is nonzero, falls back to single pages on failure, and on terminal failure releases pages already locked and clears remaining outputs before reporting memory pressure.
Exclusive state is represented by a distinct tag on device page table entries, with a scan that denies permission when any entry in the queried range carries that tag.

Snapshots install a temporary interval notifier, bound retries by a timeout, reissue faulting when busy, and only translate results after confirming the sequence remained stable while holding the mirror mutex.
The simulated device maintains free page and folio heads, a spin lock, a device memory lock, a chunk pointer table with count and capacity, and an allocation counter.
The mirror instance maintains a device reference, a flag word, a mutex, an indexed page table, and a notifier carrying the mirrored address space.
The control interface defines distinct operations for read, write, migrate to device, migrate to system, exclusive acquisition, exclusive check, snapshot, release, flags, and unlocked read.
Snapshot permission bytes distinguish error, none, zero, local versus remote private, local versus remote coherent, read versus write, and huge page sizes at two levels.
Migration descriptors use flags to indicate compound, write, migrate request, valid, and selection of system versus device owned pages including compound selection.

Chunk removal marks each chunk as removing, prunes any free entries that belong to it while holding the spin lock, then evicts, unmaps, releases the backing region for private type, and frees the descriptor, ending with empty free lists and a cleared table.
Interval notification for snapshots is delivered through an operations table whose invalidation callback updates the sequence number under the mirror mutex.

User copies after verification reads and snapshot batches report a fault error when the destination is unwritable, while allocation failures during migration report memory pressure without partial completion counts beyond verified pages.
Each migration chunk requires a virtual area that contains the current address and permits reading, with chunk boundaries clamped to the request end and to the area end.

When a large device allocation fails, the handler degrades to single page allocations across the large span, copying source contents or clearing when no source page exists, and continues after the span.
